0.note: See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm describes it as a **testimony**. This most likely means that the psalm is presenting the sufferings and defeats of the Israelites to Yahweh as a plea for him to help them on the basis that they are his covenant people. Alternate translation: [An appeal for help]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
The words **Aram Naharaim** are the name of a place.
The words **Aram Zobah** are the name of a place.
The phrase **Valley of Salt** is the name of a place.
The number **12,000** should be translated according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [twelve thousand]

Here the psalmist is providing background information about the historical circumstances in which David wrote this psalm. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

1.note: David is speaking of God as if he had **broken through** the defenses of Israel like an enemy army that is breaching a wall or battle line. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have allowed our enemies to overcome our defenses] or [you have let our defenses collapse]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please restore us]

2.note: David is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were **the earth** that Yahweh had caused to **tremble** and **broken** as in an earthquake. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have brought disaster on our nation; you have shattered it]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please heal its breaches]

David is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were land that had been damaged by an earthquake and needed to be **healed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Restore it] or [Repair the damage]

3.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **difficult** as a noun to mean difficult things or hardship. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [difficult things] or [hardship]

The psalmist is speaking of God causing his people to be confused and helpless as if he had **made** them **drink wine** that caused **staggering**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [made us confused and helpless]

4.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **a banner** is a military flag used to mark a rallying point where troops assemble for safety and coordination during battle. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a rallying flag] or [a flag to gather around for safety]

The psalmist is using **the ones fearing you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the ones who worship and honor you with reverence.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who worship you] or [those who approach you with reverence]

The psalmist is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the bow] or [on account of the bow]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote.

5.note: The expression **may be delivered** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [you, God, may deliver your beloved]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please save us]

Here, **right hand** represents power or strength. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with your might] or [with your strength]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please answer me]

The pronouns shift from **us** to **me** in this verse. The psalmist is speaking as an individual representative of the people, first using “us” to refer to the collective group, then using “me” to refer to himself as their leader. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this shift. Alternate translation: [answer me, your servant who speaks for your people]

6.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by his holy character]

This is the beginning of what God said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of God. Alternate translation: [God has spoken in his holiness, saying, “I will rejoice] or [God has spoken in his holiness, from which he says, “I will rejoice]

The implication is that David will divide Shechem as an inheritance among God’s people, demonstrating God’s sovereignty over the land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I divide Shechem as an inheritance] or [I apportion Shechem to God’s people]

7.note: David is speaking of **Ephraim** as if it were **the protection of** his **head**, that is, as if the tribe were a helmet that protected him in battle. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Ephraim protects me like a helmet] or [Ephraim is my military defense]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that while **Ephraim** was the name of one of the sons of Joseph, he and his brother, Manasseh, became patriarchs of two of the twelve tribes of Israel. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the tribe of Ephraim]
Here, **head** represents the person himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

David is speaking of **Judah** as if it were **my scepter**, the symbol of royal authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Judah, the source of my royal authority] or [Judah, the tribe from which my kingship comes]

8.note: David is speaking of **Moab** as if it were **the tub of his washing**, a basin used by a servant to wash his master’s feet. This image expresses that Moab has been reduced to servant status under God’s authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Moab is my servant] or [I will make Moab serve me like a slave]

Throwing a sandal **over Edom** was a symbolic action by which the psalmist showed that God was claiming ownership and dominion over that nation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I claim Edom as my own by throwing my sandal over it]

The psalmist is speaking to **Philistia**, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s power over the Philistines. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Philistia. Alternate translation: [Philistia will shout triumphantly over me] or [Let Philistia shout triumphantly over me]

The psalmist actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have nothing to shout about]

9.note: David is using the question form to express his need for God’s help to conquer the fortified city. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I need someone to bring me into the city of fortification!] or [Only you can bring me into the city of fortification.]

The implication is that **the city of fortification** refers to a well-fortified Edomite city, likely Petra or Bozrah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Edom’s fortified capital city]

David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Only you will lead me to Edom!] or [You alone will lead me to Edom.]

10.note: The psalmist is using the question form to express his complaint to God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [you have rejected us!] or [it seems you have rejected us.]

The psalmist is using **go out with our armies** as a common expression of the culture to mean “accompany our armies into battle” or “help us fight our enemies.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And you do not accompany our armies into battle] or [And you do not help us fight our enemies]

11.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request to God. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please give us help against the enemy] or [We beg you to give us help against the enemy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [man cannot save us] or [people cannot rescue us]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [humankind] or [people]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **futility**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the salvation of man is useless] or [for the salvation of man cannot help]

12.note: The psalmist is using **do valor** as a common expression of the culture to mean “act valiantly” or “accomplish mighty deeds.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we will act valiantly] or [we will accomplish mighty deeds]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he would literally **trample** Israel’s enemies with his feet. He means that Yahweh will decisively defeat them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will crush our adversaries] or [he will give us complete victory over our adversaries]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** twice for emphasis. He is doing this to stress that God alone will defeat the enemies. If a speaker of your language would use a repeated pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [he himself will trample our adversaries] or [it is he who will trample our adversaries]
